Banchan / Heritage

Gyeran Jjim Steamed Eggs

Soft steamed eggs, served as a comforting companion to the Korean barbecue table.

Korean · Easy · Serves 2–3 (one pot)

Jump to recipe ↓
Chapter 03 / 25 banchan recipes ↗

Behind the dish

A PLACE AT
the table.

Stream: heritage — the bubbling pot. Gyeran jjim is the banchan that arrives still boiling: eggs whipped with water and a whisper of salt, steamed in a small pot or earthenware vessel until they rise into a golden, soufflé-soft cloud, finished with scallion and sesame oil and served sizzling. It is the grill table's hot custard — the dish the table shares spoon-first straight from the vessel, and the one that vanishes in ninety seconds flat. The craft is one ratio (egg to water) and one heat law (gentle, lidded, undisturbed).

The eggs
The vessel

Set yourself up

Before you cook

  • The ratio is the recipe: 4 eggs to 160 ml liquid. More liquid and it steams to a tender soup-soft set (the pour-over-rice school); less and it goes dense and rubbery. Measure the first time; eyeball it forever after as "a little under one egg's volume of water per egg."
  • Whip it thoroughly — this is the opposite instruction from gyeran mari (#B11): 60 seconds of real whipping, incorporating air, because the steam needs that air to lift the eggs into the cloud. Strain through a fine sieve if you want the restaurant's flawlessness; skip it for the home honesty.
  • Set the steamer or the lidded pot arrangement, and start the table's rice — the eggs finish fast.

LET’S make it.

  1. 01
    The egg mixture poured into the vessel, any additions (a single anchovy, a piece of fish cake) hidden at the bottom — the treasure custom. Lid on, vessel set over the lowest heat your stove holds (or into a steamer over gentle steam). Checkpoint — nothing should happen visibly for 4–5 minutes — slow heat is the cloud's whole architecture. A rapid boil makes gray-rubbery eggs in eight minutes; resist checking.
  2. 02
    Steam gently 10–12 minutes lidded, until the center has set to a soft tremble and the edges have pulled into a puffed, risen dome. Checkpoint — the eating test at the pot: a spoon's edge should sink in with the faintest resistance and come away carrying a clean, moist, golden curd — softer than any omelet, just short of pourable. If the spoon comes away with weeping liquid, 90 more seconds; if the curd feels bouncy, it crossed into rubber — lower heat, next time.
  3. 03
    Sesame oil, scallion, sesame, chili thread over, and the pot — still bubbling at the edges from its own heat — goes to the table on its trivet. Checkpoint — the shared-pot ritual: spoons in from every side while the surface still shivers, and the bowl empties before it stops steaming. That timing is the dish's true doneness. Chef’s Note — the water temperature trick nobody mentions: warm (not cold, not hot) water whipped into the eggs saves the vessel three minutes of coming-up and cooks the eggs more evenly from the start — the same logic as starting rice in hot water. The stock variation (anchovy and kelp, a five-minute simmer) is the restaurant's depth; the water version is the home table's honest everyday — both are the same dish wearing different shoes.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Gray, rubbery eggsBoiled, not steamedLowest heat, lid, patience
Never set after 12 minutesHeat too low or too much liquidCheck the 160 ml ratio; 2 more minutes
Dense, heavy curdUnder-whipped eggsThe full 60 seconds of air
Overflowed the vesselFilled to the brimLeave 2 cm — it rises

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

  • There is no storage — gyeran jjim exists for ninety seconds and then it is a memory. Raw whipped base holds 1 day refrigerated, covered.
  • Variations: cheese folded in mid-steam (the school-café fork); saeujeot or a hidden anchovy at the pot's floor; the individual ramekin service, one per diner, is the restaurant's (and the children's) preferred format.
